ko.title: [소비자 심리학 #10] 왜 "원래 $499, 지금 $299"는 우리를 움직이는가: 프레이밍, 앵커링, 손실 회피

segments.src: > We don't judge prices and offers in a vacuum. How a choice is worded, which number we see first, and whether we feel we're gaining or losing all shape what we buy.
segments.tr: > 우리는 가격과 제안을 진공 상태에서 판단하지 않는다. 선택지가 어떤 말로 표현되는지, 어떤 숫자를 먼저 보는지, 그리고 얻는 중인지 잃는 중인지 느끼는지가 모두 무엇을 살지에 영향을 준다.

segments.src: ## Today's Concept
segments.tr: ## 오늘의 개념

segments.src: Classic economics assumed shoppers act like calculators: they compare costs and benefits and pick the best deal.
segments.tr: 고전 경제학은 소비자가 계산기처럼 행동한다고 가정했다. 즉 비용과 편익을 비교해 가장 좋은 거래를 고른다는 것이다.

segments.src: **Behavioral economics** studies what people actually do, and it finds predictable patterns that differ from that ideal.
segments.tr: **행동경제학**은 사람들이 실제로 무엇을 하는지 연구하며, 그 이상과는 다른 예측 가능한 패턴을 발견한다.

segments.src: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky did much of the founding work in the 1970s and '80s.
segments.tr: 심리학자 다니엘 카너먼과 아모스 트버스키는 1970~80년대에 이 분야의 기초 대부분을 세웠다.

segments.src: Kahneman later won the Nobel Prize in economics for it.
segments.tr: 카너먼은 이 연구로 훗날 경제학 노벨상을 받았다.

segments.src: Three of these patterns come up all the time in shopping:
segments.tr: 쇼핑에서 자주 등장하는 패턴은 세 가지다:

segments.src: Framing: the same facts, described differently**
segments.tr: 프레이밍: 같은 사실, 다르게 묘사하기**

segments.src: Two descriptions can carry the same information and still lead people to different choices.
segments.tr: 같은 정보를 담고 있어도 두 가지 설명은 사람들을 다른 선택으로 이끌 수 있다.

segments.src: In one well-known study, people rated ground beef labeled "75% lean" more favorably than beef labeled "25% fat," even though the two labels mean the same thing.
segments.tr: 유명한 연구에서 사람들은 "75% 살코기"라고 표시된 다진 소고기를, "25% 지방"이라고 표시된 것보다 더 호의적으로 평가했다. 두 표시의 의미는 같은데도 말이다.

segments.src: The frame tells us where to look.
segments.tr: 프레임은 우리가 어디를 볼지 알려준다.

segments.src: "Lean" points to the good part and "fat" points to the bad part.
segments.tr: "살코기"는 좋은 부분을, "지방"은 나쁜 부분을 가리킨다.

segments.src: Anchoring: the first number sticks**
segments.tr: 앵커링: 처음 본 숫자가 달라붙는다**

segments.src: When we estimate a value, we tend to start from whatever number we saw first (the *anchor*) and then adjust, usually not far enough.
segments.tr: 어떤 가치를 추정할 때 우리는 처음 본 숫자(*앵커*)에서 출발해 조정하는데, 보통 충분히 조정하지 못한다.

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even a number from a spinning wheel that was clearly random pulled people's later estimates toward it.
segments.tr: 트버스키와 카너먼의 실험에서는, 명백히 무작위인 돌림판의 숫자조차 이후 추정치를 그 숫자 쪽으로 끌어당겼다.

segments.src: In stores, the anchor is often the "original" price, the most expensive item on the menu, or a "suggested retail price."
segments.tr: 매장에서 앵커는 흔히 "정가", 메뉴에서 가장 비싼 항목, 또는 "권장 소비자가"다.

segments.src: Loss aversion: losing hurts more than winning feels good**
segments.tr: 손실 회피: 잃는 고통은 얻는 기쁨보다 크다**

segments.src: Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good.
segments.tr: 50달러를 잃는 것은 50달러를 줍는 기쁨보다 대개 더 나쁘게 느껴진다.

segments.src: Research estimates vary, but losses often carry roughly twice the psychological weight of equal gains.
segments.tr: 연구마다 추정치는 다르지만, 손실은 같은 크기의 이득보다 심리적 무게가 대략 두 배쯤 큰 경우가 많다.

segments.src: That's why marketers like phrases such as "Don't miss out," "Your cart is about to expire," and "You'll lose your rewards points."
segments.tr: 그래서 마케터들은 "놓치지 마세요", "장바구니 상품 곧 만료", "적립 포인트가 소멸됩니다" 같은 문구를 즐겨 쓴다.

segments.src: None of these patterns means people are foolish.
segments.tr: 이 패턴들이 사람이 어리석다는 뜻은 아니다.

segments.src: They are mental shortcuts that save effort most of the time.
segments.tr: 대부분의 경우 노력을 아껴 주는 정신적 지름길일 뿐이다.

segments.src: Marketers know about them, though, so it's worth noticing when they're being used on you.
segments.tr: 다만 마케터들은 이를 알고 있으므로, 자신에게 이런 기법이 쓰이고 있는지 알아차리는 것이 가치 있다.

segments.src: ## In Everyday Life
segments.tr: ## 일상에서

segments.src: Picture a Black Friday ad for a 65-inch TV:
segments.tr: 65인치 TV의 블랙프라이데이 광고를 떠올려 보자:

segments.src: - **"Was $499, now $299!"** The $499 works as an anchor. Next to it, $299 looks like a steal, even if the TV rarely sold for $499. (The FTC has rules against fake "former prices," but a reference price shapes your judgment either way.)
segments.tr: - **"원래 $499, 지금 $299!"** $499는 앵커 역할을 한다. 옆에 두면 $299는 TV가 실제로 $499에 거의 팔린 적이 없더라도 엄청난 특가처럼 보인다. (FTC는 가짜 "이전 가격"을 금지하는 규정을 두고 있지만, 기준 가격은 어느 쪽이든 판단에 영향을 준다.)

segments.src: - **"Save $200"** vs. **"40% off"** says the same thing in two frames. For pricier items, a dollar amount usually sounds bigger. For cheaper items, a percentage often does. Retailers tend to pick whichever frame looks larger.
segments.tr: - **"200달러 절약"** 과 **"40% 할인"** 은 같은 내용을 두 가지 프레임으로 말한다. 비싼 제품은 금액 표시가 보통 더 커 보이고, 저렴한 제품은 퍼센트 표시가 더 커 보이는 경우가 많다. 소매업체는 더 커 보이는 쪽을 골라 쓰는 경향이 있다.

segments.src: - **"Only 3 left at this price. Deal ends at midnight."** This turns *not buying* into *losing* something. Now you aren't weighing a $299 purchase. You're trying not to lose $200 in savings.
segments.tr: - **"이 가격에는 3개 남음. 행사는 자정에 종료."** 이는 *사지 않는 것*을 *무언가를 잃는 것*으로 바꾼다. 이제 당신은 299달러 구매를 저울질하는 게 아니라, 200달러의 절약을 놓치지 않으려 하고 있다.

segments.src: A simple counter-move: before you look at the "was" price, ask yourself what the TV is worth to you and what it costs at two other retailers.
segments.tr: 간단한 대응 방법: "원래 가격"을 보기 전에, 이 TV가 나에게 얼마의 가치가 있는지, 그리고 다른 두 판매점에서 얼마인지 먼저 스스로에게 물어보라.

segments.src: That way you set your own anchor.
segments.tr: 그렇게 하면 기준점을 스스로 정할 수 있다.

segments.src: ## 3-Line Summary
segments.tr: ## 3줄 요약

segments.src: 1. **Framing:** How information is worded ("75% lean" vs. "25% fat") changes choices even when the facts don't change.
segments.tr: 1. **프레이밍:** 정보를 어떻게 표현하느냐("75% 살코기" 대 "25% 지방")에 따라, 사실이 같아도 선택이 달라진다.

segments.src: 2. **Anchoring:** The first number we see, like an "original price," pulls our sense of value toward it.
segments.tr: 2. **앵커링:** "정가" 같은 처음 본 숫자가 우리의 가치 판단을 그 숫자 쪽으로 끌어당긴다.

segments.src: 3. **Loss aversion:** Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains, so "don't miss out" messages work well.
segments.tr: 3. **손실 회피:** 손실은 같은 크기의 이득보다 대략 두 배 강하게 느껴지므로, "놓치지 마세요" 메시지가 잘 먹힌다.

segments.src: ## ✅ Self-Quiz
segments.tr: ## ✅ 자가 점검 퀴즈

segments.src: **Q1.** A gym advertises "Members who skip a month lose their $100 sign-up credit."
segments.tr: **Q1.** 헬스장 광고: "한 달을 건너뛰는 회원은 $100 가입 적립금을 잃습니다."

segments.src: Which principle is it mainly using?
segments.tr: 이 광고가 주로 사용하는 원리는?

segments.src: - (a) Anchoring
segments.tr: - (a) 앵커링

segments.src: - (b) Loss aversion
segments.tr: - (b) 손실 회피

segments.src: - (c) Neither. It's just information.
segments.tr: - (c) 해당 없음. 그저 정보일 뿐이다.

segments.src: True or False:** An anchor only affects you if the number is clearly relevant to the decision.
segments.tr: 참/거짓:** 앵커는 그 숫자가 결정과 명백히 관련 있을 때만 영향을 준다.

segments.src: **Q3.** A restaurant puts a $95 steak at the top of its menu, and most diners order the $38 dish instead.
segments.tr: **Q3.** 한 식당이 메뉴 맨 위에 $95짜리 스테이크를 올려두자, 대부분의 손님은 $38짜리 요리를 주문한다.

segments.src: The $95 item is most likely working as:
segments.tr: $95짜리 항목은 주로 무엇으로 작용하고 있을 가능성이 가장 큰가?

segments.src: - (a) A frame
segments.tr: - (a) 프레임

segments.src: - (b) An anchor
segments.tr: - (b) 앵커

segments.src: - (c) A loss
segments.tr: - (c) 손실

segments.src: ## 📚 Key Terms
segments.tr: ## 📚 핵심 용어

segments.src: - **Behavioral economics:** The study of how people actually make economic decisions, including predictable departures from purely "rational" choice.
segments.tr: - **행동경제학:** 사람들이 실제로 경제적 결정을 어떻게 내리는지 연구하는 학문으로, 순수하게 "합리적인" 선택에서 예측 가능하게 벗어나는 현상을 포함한다.

segments.src: - **Framing effect:** The tendency for choices to change based on how the same information is presented.
segments.tr: - **프레이밍 효과:** 같은 정보라도 제시 방식에 따라 선택이 달라지는 경향.

segments.src: - **Anchoring:** Relying too heavily on the first number you see when estimating value.
segments.tr: - **앵커링:** 가치를 추정할 때 처음 본 숫자에 지나치게 의존하는 것.

segments.src: - **Loss aversion:** The tendency to feel losses more strongly than gains of the same size.
segments.tr: - **손실 회피:** 같은 크기의 이득보다 손실을 더 강하게 느끼는 경향.

segments.src: - **Reference price:** The price a shopper compares an offer against, such as a "was" price or MSRP.
segments.tr: - **기준 가격:** 소비자가 제안을 비교하는 기준 가격. 예를 들어 "이전 가격"이나 권장 소비자가(MSRP).

segments.src: *Answers: Q1 (b).
segments.tr: *정답: Q1 (b).

segments.src: The message is built around losing something you already have, not around gaining a benefit.
segments.tr: 이 메시지는 얻는 이익이 아니라 이미 가진 것을 잃는다는 점을 중심으로 만들어졌다.

segments.src: Q2 False.
segments.tr: Q2 거짓.

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even clearly random numbers pulled people's estimates toward them.
segments.tr: 트버스키와 카너먼의 실험에서는, 명백히 무작위인 숫자조차 사람들의 추정치를 그쪽으로 끌어당겼다.

segments.src: The expensive item sets a high reference point, so the $38 dish seems reasonable next to it.
segments.tr: 비싼 항목이 높은 기준점을 세우기 때문에, 옆에 놓인 $38 요리가 합리적으로 보이게 된다.

segments.src: This is sometimes called a "decoy" or "anchor" item.*
segments.tr: 이를 "미끼" 또는 "앵커" 항목이라고 부르기도 한다.*

zh.title: [消费心理学 #10] 为什么“原价 499，现价 299”能打动你：框架效应、锚定效应与损失厌恶

segments.src: > We don't judge prices and offers in a vacuum. How a choice is worded, which number we see first, and whether we feel we're gaining or losing all shape what we buy.
segments.tr: > 我们不是在真空中评判价格和优惠的。选择的措辞、我们先看到的数字，以及我们感觉自己是在得到还是失去，都会影响我们买什么。

segments.src: ## Today's Concept
segments.tr: ## 今日概念

segments.src: Classic economics assumed shoppers act like calculators: they compare costs and benefits and pick the best deal.
segments.tr: 传统经济学假设购物者像计算器一样：比较成本和收益，然后选出最划算的交易。

segments.src: **Behavioral economics** studies what people actually do, and it finds predictable patterns that differ from that ideal.
segments.tr: **行为经济学**研究人们实际上怎么做，并发现了与这种理想模型不同的、可预测的模式。

segments.src: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky did much of the founding work in the 1970s and '80s.
segments.tr: 心理学家丹尼尔·卡尼曼和阿莫斯·特沃斯基在 20 世纪 70 年代和 80 年代完成了这一领域的大部分奠基性工作。

segments.src: Kahneman later won the Nobel Prize in economics for it.
segments.tr: 卡尼曼后来因此获得了诺贝尔经济学奖。

segments.src: Three of these patterns come up all the time in shopping:
segments.tr: 其中有三种模式在购物中经常出现：

segments.src: Framing: the same facts, described differently**
segments.tr: 框架效应：同样的事实，不同的描述方式**

segments.src: Two descriptions can carry the same information and still lead people to different choices.
segments.tr: 两种描述可以传达相同的信息，却仍然会让人做出不同的选择。

segments.src: In one well-known study, people rated ground beef labeled "75% lean" more favorably than beef labeled "25% fat," even though the two labels mean the same thing.
segments.tr: 在一项著名研究中，人们对标着“75% 瘦肉”的牛肉评价，比标着“25% 脂肪”的牛肉更好，尽管这两个标签的含义完全相同。

segments.src: The frame tells us where to look.
segments.tr: 框架决定了我们的注意焦点。

segments.src: "Lean" points to the good part and "fat" points to the bad part.
segments.tr: “瘦肉”指向好的部分，“脂肪”指向坏的部分。

segments.src: Anchoring: the first number sticks**
segments.tr: 锚定效应：第一个数字会留下印记**

segments.src: When we estimate a value, we tend to start from whatever number we saw first (the *anchor*) and then adjust, usually not far enough.
segments.tr: 当我们估计某个价值时，往往会从最先看到的数字（即*锚点*）出发，然后进行调整，但通常调整得不够充分。

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even a number from a spinning wheel that was clearly random pulled people's later estimates toward it.
segments.tr: 在特沃斯基和卡尼曼的实验中，即使是转盘上明显随机的数字，也会把人们之后的估计拉向它。

segments.src: In stores, the anchor is often the "original" price, the most expensive item on the menu, or a "suggested retail price."
segments.tr: 在商店里，锚点通常是“原价”、菜单上最贵的商品，或是“建议零售价”。

segments.src: Loss aversion: losing hurts more than winning feels good**
segments.tr: 损失厌恶：失去的痛苦大于得到的快乐**

segments.src: Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good.
segments.tr: 丢掉 50 元通常比捡到 50 元带来的快乐更让人难受。

segments.src: Research estimates vary, but losses often carry roughly twice the psychological weight of equal gains.
segments.tr: 研究估计各不相同，但损失的心理权重往往约为等额收益的两倍。

segments.src: That's why marketers like phrases such as "Don't miss out," "Your cart is about to expire," and "You'll lose your rewards points."
segments.tr: 这就是营销人员喜欢用“别错过”“您的购物车即将过期”“您将失去积分奖励”这类说法的原因。

segments.src: None of these patterns means people are foolish.
segments.tr: 这些模式并不意味着人们愚蠢。

segments.src: They are mental shortcuts that save effort most of the time.
segments.tr: 它们是心理捷径，大多数时候能节省精力。

segments.src: Marketers know about them, though, so it's worth noticing when they're being used on you.
segments.tr: 不过，营销人员都了解这些规律，所以留意自己何时被这样对待是值得的。

segments.src: ## In Everyday Life
segments.tr: ## 日常生活中的例子

segments.src: Picture a Black Friday ad for a 65-inch TV:
segments.tr: 想象一则 65 英寸电视的黑色星期五广告：

segments.src: - **"Was $499, now $299!"** The $499 works as an anchor. Next to it, $299 looks like a steal, even if the TV rarely sold for $499. (The FTC has rules against fake "former prices," but a reference price shapes your judgment either way.)
segments.tr: - **“原价 499，现价 299！”** 499 起到锚点的作用。在它旁边，299 看起来就像捡便宜，哪怕这台电视几乎从未以 499 售出。（美国联邦贸易委员会有针对虚假“原价”的规定，但参考价格无论如何都会影响你的判断。）

segments.src: - **"Save $200"** vs. **"40% off"** says the same thing in two frames. For pricier items, a dollar amount usually sounds bigger. For cheaper items, a percentage often does. Retailers tend to pick whichever frame looks larger.
segments.tr: - **“省 200 元”** 与 **“打 6 折”** 用两种框架表达的是同一件事。对于较贵的商品，金额通常听起来更多；对于便宜的商品，百分比往往更有吸引力。零售商倾向于选择看起来更大的那种框架。

segments.src: - **"Only 3 left at this price. Deal ends at midnight."** This turns *not buying* into *losing* something. Now you aren't weighing a $299 purchase. You're trying not to lose $200 in savings.
segments.tr: - **“此价格仅剩 3 件，优惠于午夜结束。”** 这把*不买*变成了*失去*。此时你不再是在权衡一笔 299 元的消费，而是在努力不让自己失去 200 元的节省。

segments.src: A simple counter-move: before you look at the "was" price, ask yourself what the TV is worth to you and what it costs at two other retailers.
segments.tr: 一个简单的应对方法：在看“原价”之前，先问自己这台电视对你值多少钱，以及在另外两家零售商那里的价格是多少。

segments.src: ## Today's Concept
segments.tr: ## आज की अवधारणा

segments.src: Classic economics assumed shoppers act like calculators: they compare costs and benefits and pick the best deal.
segments.tr: पारंपरिक अर्थशास्त्र मानता था कि खरीदार कैलकुलेटर की तरह काम करते हैं: वे लागत और लाभ की तुलना करते हैं और सबसे अच्छा सौदा चुनते हैं।

segments.src: **Behavioral economics** studies what people actually do, and it finds predictable patterns that differ from that ideal.
segments.tr: **व्यवहारिक अर्थशास्त्र** इस बात का अध्ययन करता है कि लोग वास्तव में क्या करते हैं, और इसमें ऐसे अनुमानित पैटर्न मिलते हैं जो उस आदर्श से अलग होते हैं।

segments.src: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky did much of the founding work in the 1970s and '80s.
segments.tr: मनोवैज्ञानिक डेनियल कानेमैन और एमोस ट्वर्स्की ने 1970 और '80 के दशक में इसकी अधिकांश नींव रखी।

segments.src: Kahneman later won the Nobel Prize in economics for it.
segments.tr: बाद में कानेमैन को इसी काम के लिए अर्थशास्त्र का नोबेल पुरस्कार मिला।

segments.src: Three of these patterns come up all the time in shopping:
segments.tr: इनमें से तीन पैटर्न खरीदारी में बार-बार दिखते हैं:

segments.src: Framing: the same facts, described differently**
segments.tr: फ्रेमिंग: एक ही तथ्य, अलग तरह से वर्णित**

segments.src: Two descriptions can carry the same information and still lead people to different choices.
segments.tr: दो विवरण एक ही जानकारी दे सकते हैं और फिर भी लोगों को अलग-अलग चुनाव की ओर ले जा सकते हैं।

segments.src: In one well-known study, people rated ground beef labeled "75% lean" more favorably than beef labeled "25% fat," even though the two labels mean the same thing.
segments.tr: एक प्रसिद्ध अध्ययन में, लोगों ने "75% लीन" लेबल वाले ग्राउंड बीफ़ को "25% फ़ैट" लेबल वाले बीफ़ की तुलना में अधिक अनुकूल रेटिंग दी, जबकि दोनों लेबलों का अर्थ एक ही है।

segments.src: The frame tells us where to look.
segments.tr: फ्रेम हमें बताता है कि कहाँ देखना है।

segments.src: "Lean" points to the good part and "fat" points to the bad part.
segments.tr: "लीन" अच्छे हिस्से की ओर इशारा करता है और "फ़ैट" बुरे हिस्से की ओर।

segments.src: Anchoring: the first number sticks**
segments.tr: एंकरिंग: पहला आंकड़ा चिपक जाता है**

segments.src: When we estimate a value, we tend to start from whatever number we saw first (the *anchor*) and then adjust, usually not far enough.
segments.tr: जब हम किसी मूल्य का अनुमान लगाते हैं, तो हम आमतौर पर सबसे पहले देखे गए आंकड़े (*एंकर*) से शुरू करते हैं और फिर उसमें समायोजन करते हैं, जो आमतौर पर पर्याप्त दूर तक नहीं होता।

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even a number from a spinning wheel that was clearly random pulled people's later estimates toward it.
segments.tr: ट्वर्स्की और कानेमैन के प्रयोगों में, स्पिनिंग व्हील से निकला एक ऐसा संख्या भी, जो स्पष्ट रूप से यादृच्छिक था, लोगों के बाद के अनुमानों को उसी की ओर खींच लेता था।

segments.src: In stores, the anchor is often the "original" price, the most expensive item on the menu, or a "suggested retail price."
segments.tr: दुकानों में, एंकर अक्सर "मूल" कीमत होती है, मेन्यू पर सबसे महंगी वस्तु होती है, या "सुझाई गई खुदरा कीमत" होती है।

segments.src: Loss aversion: losing hurts more than winning feels good**
segments.tr: हानि-विमुखता: खोने की चोट, जीतने की खुशी से ज़्यादा गहरी होती है**

segments.src: Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good.
segments.tr: $50 खोना आमतौर पर $50 पाने की खुशी से ज़्यादा बुरा लगता है।

segments.src: Research estimates vary, but losses often carry roughly twice the psychological weight of equal gains.
segments.tr: शोध के अनुमान अलग-अलग हैं, लेकिन समान राशि के लाभ की तुलना में हानि का मनोवैज्ञानिक भार अक्सर लगभग दोगुना होता है।

segments.src: That's why marketers like phrases such as "Don't miss out," "Your cart is about to expire," and "You'll lose your rewards points."
segments.tr: इसीलिए विपणक "चूक मत जाइए," "आपकी कार्ट की समय-सीमा समाप्त होने वाली है," और "आप अपने रिवॉर्ड पॉइंट खो देंगे" जैसे वाक्यांश पसंद करते हैं।

segments.src: None of these patterns means people are foolish.
segments.tr: इनमें से कोई भी पैटर्न यह नहीं दिखाता कि लोग मूर्ख हैं।

segments.src: They are mental shortcuts that save effort most of the time.
segments.tr: ये मानसिक शॉर्टकट हैं जो ज़्यादातर समय प्रयास बचाते हैं।

segments.src: Marketers know about them, though, so it's worth noticing when they're being used on you.
segments.tr: फिर भी, विपणक इनके बारे में जानते हैं, इसलिए यह देखना उपयोगी है कि कब इनका इस्तेमाल आप पर हो रहा है।

segments.src: ## In Everyday Life
segments.tr: ## रोज़मर्रा की ज़िंदगी में

segments.src: Picture a Black Friday ad for a 65-inch TV:
segments.tr: 65-इंच टीवी के ब्लैक फ़्राइडे विज्ञापन की कल्पना कीजिए:

segments.src: - **"Was $499, now $299!"** The $499 works as an anchor. Next to it, $299 looks like a steal, even if the TV rarely sold for $499. (The FTC has rules against fake "former prices," but a reference price shapes your judgment either way.)
segments.tr: - **"पहले $499, अब $299!"** $499 एंकर का काम करता है। उसके बगल में $299 एक शानदार सौदा लगता है, भले ही वह टीवी शायद ही कभी $499 में बिका हो। (FTC के नियम नकली "पूर्व मूल्यों" के खिलाफ हैं, लेकिन संदर्भ मूल्य किसी भी स्थिति में आपके निर्णय को प्रभावित करता है।)

segments.src: - **"Save $200"** vs. **"40% off"** says the same thing in two frames. For pricier items, a dollar amount usually sounds bigger. For cheaper items, a percentage often does. Retailers tend to pick whichever frame looks larger.
segments.tr: - **"$200 बचाएँ"** और **"40% छूट"** एक ही बात को दो फ्रेम में कहते हैं। महंगी वस्तुओं के लिए, डॉलर की राशि आमतौर पर बड़ी लगती है। सस्ती वस्तुओं के लिए, प्रतिशत अक्सर बड़ा लगता है। खुदरा विक्रेता आमतौर पर वही फ्रेम चुनते हैं जो बड़ा दिखे।

segments.src: - **"Only 3 left at this price. Deal ends at midnight."** This turns *not buying* into *losing* something. Now you aren't weighing a $299 purchase. You're trying not to lose $200 in savings.
segments.tr: - **"इस कीमत पर सिर्फ़ 3 बचे हैं। सौदा आधी रात को खत्म होता है।"** यह *न खरीदने* को *कुछ खोने* में बदल देता है। अब आप $299 की खरीद को नहीं तौल रहे। आप $200 की बचत खोने से बचने की कोशिश कर रहे हैं।

segments.tr: एक सरल प्रतिउपाय: "पहले" वाली कीमत देखने से पहले खुद से पूछें कि इस टीवी की आपके लिए क्या कीमत है और दो अन्य खुदरा विक्रेताओं पर इसकी कीमत क्या है।

es.title: [Consumer Psychology #10] ¿Por qué te funciona «Antes $499, ahora $299»? Encuadre, anclaje y aversión a la pérdida

segments.src: > We don't judge prices and offers in a vacuum. How a choice is worded, which number we see first, and whether we feel we're gaining or losing all shape what we buy.
segments.tr: > No juzgamos los precios y las ofertas en el vacío. La forma en que se formula una elección, qué cifra vemos primero y si sentimos que estamos ganando o perdiendo, todo ello moldea lo que compramos.

segments.src: ## Today's Concept
segments.tr: ## Concepto de hoy

segments.src: Classic economics assumed shoppers act like calculators: they compare costs and benefits and pick the best deal.
segments.tr: La economía clásica suponía que los consumidores actúan como calculadoras: comparan costos y beneficios y eligen la mejor oferta.

segments.src: **Behavioral economics** studies what people actually do, and it finds predictable patterns that differ from that ideal.
segments.tr: La **economía del comportamiento** estudia lo que la gente hace realmente, y encuentra patrones predecibles que se apartan de ese ideal.

segments.src: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky did much of the founding work in the 1970s and '80s.
segments.tr: Los psicólogos Daniel Kahneman y Amos Tversky realizaron gran parte del trabajo fundacional en las décadas de 1970 y 1980.

segments.src: Kahneman later won the Nobel Prize in economics for it.
segments.tr: Kahneman recibió después el Premio Nobel de Economía por ello.

segments.src: Three of these patterns come up all the time in shopping:
segments.tr: Tres de estos patrones aparecen constantemente en las compras:

segments.src: Framing: the same facts, described differently**
segments.tr: Encuadre: los mismos hechos, descritos de otra manera**

segments.src: Two descriptions can carry the same information and still lead people to different choices.
segments.tr: Dos descripciones pueden transmitir la misma información y, aun así, llevar a las personas a elecciones distintas.

segments.src: In one well-known study, people rated ground beef labeled "75% lean" more favorably than beef labeled "25% fat," even though the two labels mean the same thing.
segments.tr: En un estudio muy conocido, la gente valoró más favorablemente la carne molida etiquetada como «75 % magra» que la etiquetada como «25 % de grasa», aunque ambas etiquetas significan lo mismo.

segments.src: The frame tells us where to look.
segments.tr: El encuadre nos indica dónde mirar.

segments.src: "Lean" points to the good part and "fat" points to the bad part.
segments.tr: «Magra» apunta a la parte buena y «grasa» apunta a la parte mala.

segments.src: Anchoring: the first number sticks**
segments.tr: Anclaje: la primera cifra se queda grabada**

segments.src: When we estimate a value, we tend to start from whatever number we saw first (the *anchor*) and then adjust, usually not far enough.
segments.tr: Cuando estimamos un valor, tendemos a partir del número que vimos primero (el *ancla*) y luego a ajustarlo, normalmente sin alejarnos lo suficiente.

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even a number from a spinning wheel that was clearly random pulled people's later estimates toward it.
segments.tr: En los experimentos de Tversky y Kahneman, incluso un número procedente de una ruleta claramente aleatoria atraía las estimaciones posteriores de las personas hacia él.

segments.src: In stores, the anchor is often the "original" price, the most expensive item on the menu, or a "suggested retail price."
segments.tr: En las tiendas, el ancla suele ser el precio «original», el artículo más caro de la carta o un «precio de venta sugerido».

segments.src: Loss aversion: losing hurts more than winning feels good**
segments.tr: Aversión a la pérdida: perder duele más de lo que ganar alegra**

segments.src: Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good.
segments.tr: Perder $50 suele sentirse peor de lo que encontrar $50 se siente bien.

segments.src: Research estimates vary, but losses often carry roughly twice the psychological weight of equal gains.
segments.tr: Las estimaciones de la investigación varían, pero las pérdidas suelen tener aproximadamente el doble de peso psicológico que las ganancias equivalentes.

segments.src: That's why marketers like phrases such as "Don't miss out," "Your cart is about to expire," and "You'll lose your rewards points."
segments.tr: Por eso a los especialistas en marketing les gustan frases como «No te lo pierdas», «Tu carrito está a punto de caducar» y «Perderás tus puntos de recompensa».

segments.src: None of these patterns means people are foolish.
segments.tr: Nada de esto significa que las personas sean tontas.

segments.src: They are mental shortcuts that save effort most of the time.
segments.tr: Son atajos mentales que ahorran esfuerzo la mayor parte del tiempo.

segments.src: Marketers know about them, though, so it's worth noticing when they're being used on you.
segments.tr: Sin embargo, los especialistas en marketing los conocen, así que conviene darse cuenta cuando los usan contigo.

segments.src: ## In Everyday Life
segments.tr: ## En la vida cotidiana

segments.src: Picture a Black Friday ad for a 65-inch TV:
segments.tr: Imagina un anuncio del Black Friday para un televisor de 65 pulgadas:

segments.src: - **"Was $499, now $299!"** The $499 works as an anchor. Next to it, $299 looks like a steal, even if the TV rarely sold for $499. (The FTC has rules against fake "former prices," but a reference price shapes your judgment either way.)
segments.tr: - **«¡Antes $499, ahora $299!»** El precio de $499 funciona como ancla. Junto a él, $299 parece una ganga, aunque el televisor casi nunca se haya vendido por $499. (La FTC tiene normas contra los «precios anteriores» falsos, pero un precio de referencia moldea tu juicio de todos modos.)

segments.src: - **"Save $200"** vs. **"40% off"** says the same thing in two frames. For pricier items, a dollar amount usually sounds bigger. For cheaper items, a percentage often does. Retailers tend to pick whichever frame looks larger.
segments.tr: - **«Ahorra $200»** frente a **«40 % de descuento»** dice lo mismo en dos encuadres. En artículos más caros, una cantidad en dólares suele sonar más grande. En artículos más baratos, suele sonar más grande un porcentaje. Los minoristas tienden a elegir el encuadre que parezca más grande.

segments.src: - **"Only 3 left at this price. Deal ends at midnight."** This turns *not buying* into *losing* something. Now you aren't weighing a $299 purchase. You're trying not to lose $200 in savings.
segments.tr: - **«Solo quedan 3 a este precio. La oferta termina a medianoche.»** Esto convierte *no comprar* en *perder* algo. Ya no estás valorando una compra de $299. Estás tratando de no perder $200 de ahorro.

segments.src: A simple counter-move: before you look at the "was" price, ask yourself what the TV is worth to you and what it costs at two other retailers.
segments.tr: Una contramedida sencilla: antes de mirar el precio «anterior», pregúntate cuánto vale el televisor para ti y cuánto cuesta en otras dos tiendas.

segments.src: That way you set your own anchor.
segments.tr: Así fijas tu propio ancla.

segments.tr: 1. **Encuadre:** Cómo se formula la información («75 % magra» frente a «25 % de grasa») cambia las elecciones aunque los hechos no cambien.

segments.src: - **Framing effect:** The tendency for choices to change based on how the same information is presented.

segments.src: - **Anchoring:** Relying too heavily on the first number you see when estimating value.
segments.tr: - **Anclaje:** Depender demasiado del primer número que se ve al estimar un valor.

segments.src: - **Loss aversion:** The tendency to feel losses more strongly than gains of the same size.
segments.tr: - **Aversión a la pérdida:** Tendencia a sentir las pérdidas con más intensidad que las ganancias de igual tamaño.

segments.src: - **Reference price:** The price a shopper compares an offer against, such as a "was" price or MSRP.

fr.title: [Psychologie du consommateur n°10] Pourquoi « Était 499 $, maintenant 299 $ » vous influence : cadrage, ancrage et aversion à la perte

segments.src: > We don't judge prices and offers in a vacuum. How a choice is worded, which number we see first, and whether we feel we're gaining or losing all shape what we buy.
segments.tr: > Nous ne jugeons pas les prix et les offres dans le vide. La manière dont un choix est formulé, le chiffre que nous voyons en premier et le sentiment de gagner ou de perdre façonnent tous ce que nous achetons.

segments.src: ## Today's Concept
segments.tr: ## Concept du jour

segments.src: Classic economics assumed shoppers act like calculators: they compare costs and benefits and pick the best deal.
segments.tr: L'économie classique supposait que les consommateurs agissent comme des calculatrices : ils comparent coûts et bénéfices et choisissent la meilleure affaire.

segments.src: **Behavioral economics** studies what people actually do, and it finds predictable patterns that differ from that ideal.
segments.tr: **L'économie comportementale** étudie ce que les gens font réellement, et elle met en évidence des schémas prévisibles qui s'écartent de cet idéal.

segments.src: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky did much of the founding work in the 1970s and '80s.
segments.tr: Les psychologues Daniel Kahneman et Amos Tversky ont accompli l'essentiel du travail fondateur dans les années 1970 et 1980.

segments.src: Kahneman later won the Nobel Prize in economics for it.
segments.tr: Kahneman a ensuite reçu le prix Nobel d'économie pour ces travaux.

segments.src: Three of these patterns come up all the time in shopping:
segments.tr: Trois de ces schémas reviennent constamment dans les achats :

segments.src: Framing: the same facts, described differently**
segments.tr: Cadrage : les mêmes faits, décrits différemment**

segments.src: Two descriptions can carry the same information and still lead people to different choices.
segments.tr: Deux descriptions peuvent contenir la même information et pourtant conduire les gens à des choix différents.

segments.src: In one well-known study, people rated ground beef labeled "75% lean" more favorably than beef labeled "25% fat," even though the two labels mean the same thing.
segments.tr: Dans une étude bien connue, des personnes ont jugé plus favorablement de la viande hachée étiquetée « 75 % de viande maigre » que de la viande étiquetée « 25 % de matière grasse », alors que les deux étiquettes signifient exactement la même chose.

segments.src: The frame tells us where to look.
segments.tr: Le cadrage indique où regarder.

segments.src: "Lean" points to the good part and "fat" points to the bad part.
segments.tr: « Maigre » attire l'attention sur la bonne part, et « matière grasse » sur la mauvaise.

segments.src: Anchoring: the first number sticks**
segments.tr: Ancrage : le premier chiffre reste en tête**

segments.src: When we estimate a value, we tend to start from whatever number we saw first (the *anchor*) and then adjust, usually not far enough.
segments.tr: Lorsque nous estimons une valeur, nous avons tendance à partir du premier chiffre que nous avons vu (l'*ancre*), puis à l'ajuster, généralement pas assez.

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even a number from a spinning wheel that was clearly random pulled people's later estimates toward it.
segments.tr: Dans les expériences de Tversky et Kahneman, même un nombre issu d'une roue de loterie, manifestement aléatoire, a attiré les estimations ultérieures des participants vers lui.

segments.src: In stores, the anchor is often the "original" price, the most expensive item on the menu, or a "suggested retail price."
segments.tr: En magasin, l'ancre est souvent le prix « d'origine », l'article le plus cher de la gamme ou un « prix de vente conseillé ».

segments.src: Loss aversion: losing hurts more than winning feels good**
segments.tr: Aversion à la perte : perdre fait plus mal que gagner ne procure de plaisir**

segments.src: Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good.
segments.tr: Perdre 50 $ est généralement plus désagréable que trouver 50 $ n'est agréable.

segments.src: Research estimates vary, but losses often carry roughly twice the psychological weight of equal gains.
segments.tr: Les estimations de la recherche varient, mais les pertes ont souvent un poids psychologique environ deux fois supérieur à celui de gains équivalents.

segments.src: That's why marketers like phrases such as "Don't miss out," "Your cart is about to expire," and "You'll lose your rewards points."
segments.tr: C'est pourquoi les professionnels du marketing aiment les formules comme « Ne manquez pas cette occasion », « Votre panier va bientôt expirer » ou « Vous allez perdre vos points de fidélité ».

segments.src: None of these patterns means people are foolish.
segments.tr: Rien de tout cela ne signifie que les gens sont idiots.

segments.src: They are mental shortcuts that save effort most of the time.
segments.tr: Ce sont des raccourcis mentaux qui économisent de l'effort la plupart du temps.

segments.src: Marketers know about them, though, so it's worth noticing when they're being used on you.
segments.tr: Les spécialistes du marketing connaissent ces mécanismes, il vaut donc la peine de remarquer quand on les utilise contre vous.

segments.src: ## In Everyday Life
segments.tr: ## Dans la vie quotidienne

segments.src: Picture a Black Friday ad for a 65-inch TV:
segments.tr: Imaginez une publicité du Black Friday pour un téléviseur de 65 pouces :

segments.src: - **"Was $499, now $299!"** The $499 works as an anchor. Next to it, $299 looks like a steal, even if the TV rarely sold for $499. (The FTC has rules against fake "former prices," but a reference price shapes your judgment either way.)
segments.tr: - **« Était 499 $, maintenant 299 $ ! »** Le prix de 499 $ sert d'ancre. À côté, 299 $ paraît une bonne affaire, même si ce téléviseur ne s'est presque jamais vendu 499 $. (La FTC interdit les faux « anciens prix », mais un prix de référence influence votre jugement dans tous les cas.)

segments.src: - **"Save $200"** vs. **"40% off"** says the same thing in two frames. For pricier items, a dollar amount usually sounds bigger. For cheaper items, a percentage often does. Retailers tend to pick whichever frame looks larger.
segments.tr: - **« Économisez 200 $ »** et **« 40 % de réduction »** disent la même chose sous deux formes. Pour les articles plus chers, un montant en dollars semble généralement plus important. Pour les articles moins chers, un pourcentage paraît souvent plus important. Les détaillants choisissent en général la formulation qui semble la plus avantageuse.

segments.src: - **"Only 3 left at this price. Deal ends at midnight."** This turns *not buying* into *losing* something. Now you aren't weighing a $299 purchase. You're trying not to lose $200 in savings.
segments.tr: - **« Plus que 3 à ce prix. L'offre se termine à minuit. »** Cela transforme *ne pas acheter* en *perdre* quelque chose. Vous ne pesez plus un achat de 299 $. Vous essayez d'éviter de perdre 200 $ d'économies.

segments.src: A simple counter-move: before you look at the "was" price, ask yourself what the TV is worth to you and what it costs at two other retailers.
segments.tr: Une contre-stratégie simple : avant de regarder le prix « d'origine », demandez-vous ce que le téléviseur vaut pour vous et combien il coûte chez deux autres revendeurs.

segments.src: That way you set your own anchor.
segments.tr: Vous fixez ainsi votre propre ancre.

segments.tr: ## Résumé en 3 lignes

segments.tr: 1. **Cadrage :** la formulation de l'information (« 75 % maigre » contre « 25 % matière grasse ») modifie les choix alors que les faits ne changent pas.

segments.src: 2. **Anchoring:** The first number we see, like an "original price," pulls our sense of value toward it.
segments.tr: 2. **Ancrage :** le premier chiffre que nous voyons, comme un « prix d'origine », attire notre perception de la valeur vers lui.

segments.src: 3. **Loss aversion:** Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains, so "don't miss out" messages work well.
segments.tr: 3. **Aversion à la perte :** les pertes semblent environ deux fois plus fortes que des gains équivalents, c'est pourquoi les messages du type « ne manquez pas » fonctionnent bien.

in.title: [Psikologi Konsumen #10] Mengapa "Dulu $499, Sekarang $299" Memengaruhimu: Pembingkaian, Penjangkaran, dan Keengganan Kehilangan

segments.src: > We don't judge prices and offers in a vacuum. How a choice is worded, which number we see first, and whether we feel we're gaining or losing all shape what we buy.
segments.tr: > Kita tidak menilai harga dan penawaran secara terpisah. Cara sebuah pilihan dirumuskan, angka mana yang kita lihat lebih dulu, dan apakah kita merasa sedang untung atau rugi, semuanya membentuk apa yang kita beli.

segments.src: ## Today's Concept
segments.tr: ## Konsep Hari Ini

segments.src: Classic economics assumed shoppers act like calculators: they compare costs and benefits and pick the best deal.
segments.tr: Ekonomi klasik berasumsi pembeli bertindak seperti kalkulator: mereka membandingkan biaya dan manfaat lalu memilih kesepakatan terbaik.

segments.src: **Behavioral economics** studies what people actually do, and it finds predictable patterns that differ from that ideal.
segments.tr: **Ekonomi perilaku** mempelajari apa yang sebenarnya dilakukan orang, dan menemukan pola yang dapat diprediksi yang berbeda dari kondisi ideal tersebut.

segments.src: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky did much of the founding work in the 1970s and '80s.
segments.tr: Psikolog Daniel Kahneman dan Amos Tversky melakukan sebagian besar kerja fondasinya pada tahun 1970-an dan 1980-an.

segments.src: Kahneman later won the Nobel Prize in economics for it.
segments.tr: Kahneman kemudian memenangkan Hadiah Nobel di bidang ekonomi atas karya ini.

segments.src: Three of these patterns come up all the time in shopping:
segments.tr: Tiga pola ini sering muncul dalam belanja:

segments.src: Framing: the same facts, described differently**
segments.tr: Pembingkaian: fakta yang sama, dikemas berbeda**

segments.src: Two descriptions can carry the same information and still lead people to different choices.
segments.tr: Dua deskripsi bisa memuat informasi yang sama namun tetap membuat orang memilih berbeda.

segments.src: In one well-known study, people rated ground beef labeled "75% lean" more favorably than beef labeled "25% fat," even though the two labels mean the same thing.
segments.tr: Dalam satu studi terkenal, orang menilai daging sapi giling berlabel "75% lean" lebih baik daripada yang berlabel "25% fat", padahal kedua label itu berarti sama.

segments.src: The frame tells us where to look.
segments.tr: Bingkai memberi tahu kita ke mana harus melihat.

segments.src: "Lean" points to the good part and "fat" points to the bad part.
segments.tr: "Lean" mengarahkan perhatian ke bagian yang baik, dan "fat" mengarahkan ke bagian yang buruk.

segments.src: Anchoring: the first number sticks**
segments.tr: Penjangkaran: angka pertama akan melekat**

segments.src: When we estimate a value, we tend to start from whatever number we saw first (the *anchor*) and then adjust, usually not far enough.
segments.tr: Saat memperkirakan suatu nilai, kita cenderung mulai dari angka apa pun yang pertama kali kita lihat (*anchor*), lalu menyesuaikannya, biasanya tidak cukup jauh.

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even a number from a spinning wheel that was clearly random pulled people's later estimates toward it.
segments.tr: Dalam eksperimen Tversky dan Kahneman, bahkan angka dari roda berputar yang jelas acak tetap menarik perkiraan orang berikutnya ke arahnya.

segments.src: In stores, the anchor is often the "original" price, the most expensive item on the menu, or a "suggested retail price."
segments.tr: Di toko, jangkar sering berupa harga "asli", barang termahal di menu, atau "harga eceran yang disarankan".

segments.src: Loss aversion: losing hurts more than winning feels good**
segments.tr: Keengganan kehilangan (loss aversion): kehilangan terasa lebih menyakitkan daripada rasa senang saat mendapat untung**

segments.src: Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good.
segments.tr: Kehilangan uang $50 biasanya terasa lebih buruk daripada menemukan uang $50 terasa menyenangkan.

segments.src: Research estimates vary, but losses often carry roughly twice the psychological weight of equal gains.
segments.tr: Perkiraan penelitian bervariasi, tetapi kerugian sering membawa bobot psikologis sekitar dua kali lipat dari keuntungan yang setara.

segments.src: That's why marketers like phrases such as "Don't miss out," "Your cart is about to expire," and "You'll lose your rewards points."
segments.tr: Itulah sebabnya pemasar menyukai frasa seperti "Jangan sampai ketinggalan", "Keranjangmu hampir kedaluwarsa", dan "Poin reward kamu akan hangus".

segments.src: None of these patterns means people are foolish.
segments.tr: Tidak ada pola ini yang berarti orang itu bodoh.

segments.src: They are mental shortcuts that save effort most of the time.
segments.tr: Pola ini adalah jalan pintas mental yang menghemat usaha sebagian besar waktu.

segments.src: Marketers know about them, though, so it's worth noticing when they're being used on you.
segments.tr: Namun, pemasar memahami hal ini, jadi perlu disadari saat hal ini dipakai terhadapmu.

segments.src: ## In Everyday Life
segments.tr: ## Dalam Kehidupan Sehari-hari

segments.src: Picture a Black Friday ad for a 65-inch TV:
segments.tr: Bayangkan iklan Black Friday untuk TV 65 inci:

segments.src: - **"Was $499, now $299!"** The $499 works as an anchor. Next to it, $299 looks like a steal, even if the TV rarely sold for $499. (The FTC has rules against fake "former prices," but a reference price shapes your judgment either way.)
segments.tr: - **"Dulu $499, sekarang $299!"** Angka $499 berfungsi sebagai jangkar. Di sampingnya, $299 terlihat seperti obral, meskipun TV itu jarang terjual seharga $499. (FTC memiliki aturan terhadap "harga lama" palsu, tetapi harga acuan tetap membentuk penilaianmu.)

segments.src: - **"Save $200"** vs. **"40% off"** says the same thing in two frames. For pricier items, a dollar amount usually sounds bigger. For cheaper items, a percentage often does. Retailers tend to pick whichever frame looks larger.
segments.tr: - **"Hemat $200"** dan **"Diskon 40%"** menyampaikan hal yang sama dalam dua bingkai. Untuk barang yang lebih mahal, nominal uang biasanya terdengar lebih besar. Untuk barang yang lebih murah, persentase sering terdengar lebih besar. Peritel cenderung memilih bingkai yang terlihat lebih besar.

segments.src: - **"Only 3 left at this price. Deal ends at midnight."** This turns *not buying* into *losing* something. Now you aren't weighing a $299 purchase. You're trying not to lose $200 in savings.
segments.tr: - **"Tersisa 3 unit dengan harga ini. Promo berakhir tengah malam."** Ini mengubah *tidak membeli* menjadi *kehilangan* sesuatu. Sekarang kamu bukan sedang menimbang pembelian $299, melainkan berusaha agar tidak kehilangan penghematan $200.

segments.src: A simple counter-move: before you look at the "was" price, ask yourself what the TV is worth to you and what it costs at two other retailers.
segments.tr: Langkah balasan sederhana: sebelum melihat harga "dulu", tanyakan pada dirimu sendiri berapa nilai TV itu bagimu dan berapa harganya di dua peritel lain.

segments.src: That way you set your own anchor.
segments.tr: Dengan begitu, kamu menetapkan jangkar milikmu sendiri.

segments.src: ## 3-Line Summary
segments.tr: ## Ringkasan 3 Baris

segments.tr: 1. **Pembingkaian:** Cara informasi disampaikan ("75% lean" vs. "25% fat") mengubah pilihan meskipun faktanya tidak berubah.

segments.src: 2. **Anchoring:** The first number we see, like an "original price," pulls our sense of value toward it.
segments.tr: 2. **Penjangkaran:** Angka pertama yang kita lihat, seperti "harga asli", menarik rasa nilai kita ke arahnya.

segments.src: 3. **Loss aversion:** Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains, so "don't miss out" messages work well.
segments.tr: 3. **Keengganan kehilangan:** Kerugian cenderung terasa sekitar dua kali lebih kuat daripada keuntungan yang setara, sehingga pesan "jangan sampai ketinggalan" efektif.

de.title: [Konsumpsychologie #10] Warum „Früher 499 $, jetzt 299 $“ bei dir wirkt: Framing, Ankereffekt und Verlustaversion

segments.src: > We don't judge prices and offers in a vacuum. How a choice is worded, which number we see first, and whether we feel we're gaining or losing all shape what we buy.
segments.tr: > Wir beurteilen Preise und Angebote nicht im luftleeren Raum. Wie eine Wahl formuliert ist, welche Zahl wir zuerst sehen und ob wir das Gefühl haben, etwas zu gewinnen oder zu verlieren, prägt, was wir kaufen.

segments.src: ## Today's Concept
segments.tr: ## Das heutige Konzept

segments.src: Classic economics assumed shoppers act like calculators: they compare costs and benefits and pick the best deal.
segments.tr: Die klassische Ökonomie ging davon aus, dass Käufer wie Taschenrechner handeln: Sie vergleichen Kosten und Nutzen und wählen das beste Angebot.

segments.src: **Behavioral economics** studies what people actually do, and it finds predictable patterns that differ from that ideal.
segments.tr: **Verhaltensökonomie** untersucht, was Menschen tatsächlich tun, und findet dabei vorhersagbare Muster, die von diesem Ideal abweichen.

segments.src: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky did much of the founding work in the 1970s and '80s.
segments.tr: Die Psychologen Daniel Kahneman und Amos Tversky haben in den 1970er- und 1980er-Jahren das Fundament dafür gelegt.

segments.src: Kahneman later won the Nobel Prize in economics for it.
segments.tr: Kahneman erhielt dafür später den Nobelpreis für Wirtschaftswissenschaften.

segments.src: Three of these patterns come up all the time in shopping:
segments.tr: Drei dieser Muster tauchen beim Einkaufen ständig auf:

segments.src: Framing: the same facts, described differently**
segments.tr: Framing: dieselben Fakten, anders beschrieben**

segments.src: Two descriptions can carry the same information and still lead people to different choices.
segments.tr: Zwei Beschreibungen können dieselbe Information enthalten und dennoch zu unterschiedlichen Entscheidungen führen.

segments.src: In one well-known study, people rated ground beef labeled "75% lean" more favorably than beef labeled "25% fat," even though the two labels mean the same thing.
segments.tr: In einer bekannten Studie bewerteten Menschen Hackfleisch mit der Angabe „75 % mager“ günstiger als Hackfleisch mit der Angabe „25 % Fett“, obwohl beide Angaben dasselbe bedeuten.

segments.src: The frame tells us where to look.
segments.tr: Das Framing legt fest, wohin wir schauen.

segments.src: "Lean" points to the good part and "fat" points to the bad part.
segments.tr: „Mager“ lenkt den Blick auf den guten Teil, „Fett“ auf den schlechten.

segments.src: Anchoring: the first number sticks**
segments.tr: Ankereffekt: die erste Zahl bleibt haften**

segments.src: When we estimate a value, we tend to start from whatever number we saw first (the *anchor*) and then adjust, usually not far enough.
segments.tr: Wenn wir einen Wert schätzen, orientieren wir uns meist an der Zahl, die wir zuerst gesehen haben (dem *Anker*), und passen sie dann an, meist nicht weit genug.

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even a number from a spinning wheel that was clearly random pulled people's later estimates toward it.
segments.tr: In den Experimenten von Tversky und Kahneman zog selbst eine Zahl von einem Glücksrad, die eindeutig zufällig war, die späteren Schätzungen der Menschen zu sich heran.

segments.src: In stores, the anchor is often the "original" price, the most expensive item on the menu, or a "suggested retail price."
segments.tr: In Geschäften ist der Anker oft der „Originalpreis“, das teuerste Produkt im Angebot oder eine „unverbindliche Preisempfehlung“.

segments.src: Loss aversion: losing hurts more than winning feels good**
segments.tr: Verlustaversion: Verlieren schmerzt stärker, als Gewinnen erfreut**

segments.src: Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good.
segments.tr: Einen Verlust von 50 $ zu erleiden fühlt sich meist schlimmer an, als das Finden von 50 $ sich gut anfühlt.

segments.src: Research estimates vary, but losses often carry roughly twice the psychological weight of equal gains.
segments.tr: Die Schätzungen der Forschung variieren, aber Verluste haben oft ungefähr das doppelte psychologische Gewicht gleich großer Gewinne.

segments.src: That's why marketers like phrases such as "Don't miss out," "Your cart is about to expire," and "You'll lose your rewards points."
segments.tr: Deshalb setzen Marketer gern Sätze ein wie „Verpass das nicht“, „Dein Warenkorb läuft bald ab“ und „Du verlierst deine Bonuspunkte“.

segments.src: None of these patterns means people are foolish.
segments.tr: Keines dieser Muster bedeutet, dass Menschen dumm sind.

segments.src: They are mental shortcuts that save effort most of the time.
segments.tr: Es sind mentale Abkürzungen, die meistens Mühe sparen.

segments.src: Marketers know about them, though, so it's worth noticing when they're being used on you.
segments.tr: Marketer kennen sie jedoch, deshalb lohnt es sich zu bemerken, wenn sie bei dir angewendet werden.

segments.src: ## In Everyday Life
segments.tr: ## Im Alltag

segments.src: Picture a Black Friday ad for a 65-inch TV:
segments.tr: Stell dir eine Black-Friday-Anzeige für einen 65-Zoll-Fernseher vor:

segments.src: - **"Was $499, now $299!"** The $499 works as an anchor. Next to it, $299 looks like a steal, even if the TV rarely sold for $499. (The FTC has rules against fake "former prices," but a reference price shapes your judgment either way.)
segments.tr: - **„Früher 499 $, jetzt 299 $!“** Die 499 $ wirken als Anker. Daneben sehen 299 $ nach einem Schnäppchen aus, auch wenn der Fernseher selten für 499 $ verkauft wurde. (Die US-Handelsaufsicht FTC hat Regeln gegen erfundene „früheren Preise“, aber ein Referenzpreis prägt dein Urteil in jedem Fall.)

segments.src: - **"Save $200"** vs. **"40% off"** says the same thing in two frames. For pricier items, a dollar amount usually sounds bigger. For cheaper items, a percentage often does. Retailers tend to pick whichever frame looks larger.
segments.tr: - **„200 $ sparen“** vs. **„40 % Rabatt“** sagt in zwei Rahmen dasselbe. Bei teureren Artikeln klingt ein Dollarbetrag meist größer. Bei günstigeren Artikeln wirkt oft ein Prozentsatz größer. Händler wählen tendenziell den Rahmen, der größer aussieht.

segments.src: - **"Only 3 left at this price. Deal ends at midnight."** This turns *not buying* into *losing* something. Now you aren't weighing a $299 purchase. You're trying not to lose $200 in savings.
segments.tr: - **„Nur noch 3 zu diesem Preis. Angebot endet um Mitternacht.“** Das macht *Nichtkaufen* zu *Verlieren*. Du wägst nicht mehr einen Kauf für 299 $ ab, sondern versuchst, 200 $ Ersparnis nicht zu verlieren.

segments.src: A simple counter-move: before you look at the "was" price, ask yourself what the TV is worth to you and what it costs at two other retailers.
segments.tr: Ein einfacher Gegenzug: Bevor du auf den „früheren“ Preis schaust, frag dich, was dir der Fernseher wert ist und was er bei zwei anderen Händlern kostet.

segments.src: That way you set your own anchor.
segments.tr: So setzt du deinen eigenen Anker.

segments.src: ## 3-Line Summary
segments.tr: ## Zusammenfassung in 3 Zeilen

segments.src: 1. **Framing:** How information is worded ("75% lean" vs. "25% fat") changes choices even when the facts don't change.
segments.tr: 1. **Framing:** Wie Informationen formuliert sind („75 % mager“ vs. „25 % Fett“), verändert Entscheidungen, auch wenn sich die Fakten nicht ändern.

segments.src: 2. **Anchoring:** The first number we see, like an "original price," pulls our sense of value toward it.
segments.tr: 2. **Ankereffekt:** Die erste Zahl, die wir sehen, etwa ein „Originalpreis“, zieht unser Wertgefühl zu sich hin.

segments.src: 3. **Loss aversion:** Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains, so "don't miss out" messages work well.
segments.tr: 3. **Verlustaversion:** Verluste fühlen sich ungefähr doppelt so stark an wie gleich große Gewinne, deshalb wirken Botschaften wie „Verpass das nicht“ gut.

segments.src: ## 3-Line Summary
segments.tr: ## Tóm tắt 3 dòng

segments.src: 1. **Framing:** How information is worded ("75% lean" vs. "25% fat") changes choices even when the facts don't change.
segments.tr: 1. **Khung diễn đạt:** Cách diễn đạt thông tin ("75% nạc" so với "25% mỡ") làm thay đổi lựa chọn dù sự thật không đổi.

segments.src: 2. **Anchoring:** The first number we see, like an "original price," pulls our sense of value toward it.
segments.tr: 2. **Neo giá:** Con số đầu tiên ta thấy, như "giá gốc", kéo cảm nhận của ta về giá trị về phía nó.

segments.src: 3. **Loss aversion:** Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains, so "don't miss out" messages work well.
segments.tr: 3. **Né tránh mất mát:** Mất mát thường cảm thấy mạnh gấp khoảng hai lần lợi ích cùng độ lớn, nên thông điệp "đừng bỏ lỡ" hiệu quả.

segments.src: ## ✅ Self-Quiz
segments.tr: ## ✅ Tự kiểm tra

segments.src: **Q1.** A gym advertises "Members who skip a month lose their $100 sign-up credit."
segments.tr: **Q1.** Một phòng gym quảng cáo "Hội viên nào bỏ tập một tháng sẽ mất khoản tín dụng đăng ký 100 USD."

segments.src: Which principle is it mainly using?
segments.tr: Nguyên tắc chính mà nó sử dụng là gì?

segments.src: - (a) Anchoring
segments.tr: - (a) Neo giá

segments.src: - (b) Loss aversion
segments.tr: - (b) Né tránh mất mát

segments.src: - (c) Neither. It's just information.
segments.tr: - (c) Không gì cả. Đó chỉ là thông tin.

segments.src: True or False:** An anchor only affects you if the number is clearly relevant to the decision.
segments.tr: Đúng hay Sai:** Một neo chỉ ảnh hưởng đến bạn nếu con số đó rõ ràng liên quan đến quyết định.

segments.src: **Q3.** A restaurant puts a $95 steak at the top of its menu, and most diners order the $38 dish instead.
segments.tr: **Q3.** Một nhà hàng đặt món bò bít tết 95 USD ở đầu thực đơn, và phần lớn thực khách lại gọi món 38 USD.

segments.src: The $95 item is most likely working as:
segments.tr: Món 95 USD nhiều khả năng đang đóng vai trò là:

segments.src: - (a) A frame
segments.tr: - (a) Một khung diễn đạt

segments.src: - (b) An anchor
segments.tr: - (b) Một neo

segments.src: - (c) A loss
segments.tr: - (c) Một khoản mất mát

segments.src: ## 📚 Key Terms
segments.tr: ## 📚 Thuật ngữ chính

segments.src: - **Behavioral economics:** The study of how people actually make economic decisions, including predictable departures from purely "rational" choice.
segments.tr: - **Kinh tế học hành vi:** Nghiên cứu cách con người thực sự đưa ra quyết định kinh tế, bao gồm những sai lệch có thể dự đoán so với lựa chọn "duy lý" thuần túy.

segments.src: - **Framing effect:** The tendency for choices to change based on how the same information is presented.
segments.tr: - **Hiệu ứng khung diễn đạt:** Xu hướng lựa chọn thay đổi tùy theo cách trình bày cùng một thông tin.

segments.src: - **Anchoring:** Relying too heavily on the first number you see when estimating value.
segments.tr: - **Neo giá (anchoring):** Dựa quá nhiều vào con số đầu tiên thấy khi ước lượng giá trị.

segments.src: - **Loss aversion:** The tendency to feel losses more strongly than gains of the same size.
segments.tr: - **Né tránh mất mát:** Xu hướng cảm nhận mất mát mạnh hơn lợi ích có cùng độ lớn.

segments.src: - **Reference price:** The price a shopper compares an offer against, such as a "was" price or MSRP.
segments.tr: - **Giá tham chiếu:** Mức giá mà người mua so sánh một ưu đãi với, chẳng hạn giá "gốc" hoặc MSRP (giá bán lẻ đề xuất của nhà sản xuất).

segments.src: *Answers: Q1 (b).
segments.tr: *Đáp án: Q1 (b).

segments.src: The message is built around losing something you already have, not around gaining a benefit.
segments.tr: Thông điệp xoay quanh việc mất đi thứ bạn đã có, chứ không phải việc đạt thêm lợi ích.

segments.src: Q2 False.
segments.tr: Q2 Sai.

segments.src: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiments, even clearly random numbers pulled people's estimates toward them.
segments.tr: Trong thí nghiệm của Tversky và Kahneman, ngay cả những con số rõ ràng là ngẫu nhiên cũng kéo ước lượng của người tham gia về phía chúng.

segments.src: The expensive item sets a high reference point, so the $38 dish seems reasonable next to it.
segments.tr: Món đắt tiền đặt ra một điểm tham chiếu cao, nên món 38 USD có vẻ hợp lý khi đặt cạnh nó.

segments.src: This is sometimes called a "decoy" or "anchor" item.*
segments.tr: Đôi khi điều này được gọi là món "mồi" (decoy) hoặc món "neo".*
